title: 0/1 knapsack
prompt: Given a capacity and two parallel slices weights and values, return the greatest total value you can carry, taking each item at most once. Items are indivisible: you either take one or you leave it. The tests include 2001 items with capacity 5000, so enumerating subsets is out, and they check the two classic wrong answers: reusing an item, and taking items greedily by value per unit weight.
explanation: best[c] is the most value that fits in capacity exactly c or less, over the items considered so far. Adding item i means best[c] = max(best[c], best[c-w] + v), which is O(nW) time and, with a single row, O(W) space. The direction of the inner loop is the whole trick: counting c downward means best[c-w] is still the row from before item i was added, so item i can enter the answer only once. Counting upward reads a cell that may already contain item i, which is exactly the unbounded knapsack recurrence and is why the single-item test returns 20 instead of 10. Greedy by value/weight fails because the leftover capacity has value too: item 0 has the best ratio and the worst fit. Note O(nW) is pseudo-polynomial, not polynomial, since W is exponential in the bits used to write it down.
hints: One number per capacity is enough state if you fold the items in one at a time.
Write the recurrence for 'capacity c, first i items' and then ask what you actually need from row i-1.
The order you visit capacities decides whether an item can be picked twice.

title: Longest palindromic substring in linear time
prompt: Return a longest palindromic substring of s. Ties are fine: any longest one is accepted, and the empty string maps to the empty string. It has to be linear: one test is 200000 identical letters and another is 400001 characters palindromic across a single middle letter, so expanding around every centre costs O(n^2) and never finishes. Even-length palindromes count.
explanation: This is Manacher. Two ideas do the work. First, interleaving a separator between every pair of characters (and at both ends) makes every palindrome odd-length, so even and odd centres stop being separate cases; a palindrome of radius r in the padded string is a palindrome of length r in the original, starting at (centre - r) / 2. Second, keep the palindrome that reaches furthest right, as a centre and a right edge. For a new position i inside that palindrome, the mirror position 2*centre - i has already been measured, and its radius is valid for i up to the point where it would cross the right edge, so start there and only then expand character by character. Every extra character examined pushes the right edge further right, and the right edge never moves back, so the total expansion work over the whole scan is O(n). The alternative linear-ish answers are binary search on length over a rolling hash, or a suffix automaton of s and its reverse; both are more machinery for the same result.
hints: Get rid of the even/odd distinction before you optimise anything: pad the string so every centre is a character.
Remember the palindrome whose right edge is furthest along, and what its mirror tells you about a position inside it.
A mirrored radius is only trustworthy up to that right edge; past it you have to compare characters yourself.

title: Skyline by sweeping x
prompt: Given buildings as [left, right, height] rectangles standing on the ground, return the outline as key points [x, height], left to right: a point wherever the outline's height changes, and a final point at height 0. No two consecutive points may repeat a height, and buildings that merely touch produce no step. The tests run 200000 nested buildings, so re-scanning the buildings at each x does not finish.
explanation: Sweep x over the sorted set of edges, keeping the live buildings in a max-heap keyed on height and carrying the x where each ends. At a given x: push everything that starts here, drop heap tops whose right edge is at or before x, then read the top as the current outline height and emit a point only when it differs from the last one emitted. Doing all the pushes before all the reads is what makes a building that ends exactly where the next begins produce no step; settling the ends first would drop to 0 and back up at the same x. Removing an arbitrary building from a binary heap is not supported, hence lazy deletion: a building that ended is only discarded when it surfaces, which is fine because a stale entry can never be the answer once its right edge is behind the sweep. Sorting dominates at O(n log n). Divide and conquer, merging two skylines like mergesort, is the other standard answer at the same cost.
hints: The only x values that can matter are building edges, so sort those and step through them.
You need the tallest live building at each stop, and you never need to delete from the middle: a finished building can be dropped when it reaches the top.
Decide what happens at an x that is both a right edge and a left edge before you write the loop.
